front: Brønsted–Lowry acid and base?
back: Acid: proton donor. Base: proton acceptor.

front: Conjugate acid–base pair?
back: Two species differing by one H⁺ (e.g. CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻).

front: pH definition?
back: pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; [H⁺] = 10^−pH.

front: Kw at 298 K?
Strong vs weak acid?
back: Strong: fully ionised. Weak: partially ionised (equilibrium).

front: Neutralisation products?
back: Base → salt + water; carbonate → salt + water + CO₂; metal → salt + H₂.

front: (HL) Ka and pH of a weak acid?
(HL) Ka and Kb of a conjugate pair?
back: Ka × Kb = Kw; pKa + pKb = 14.00.

front: (HL) pH of salts?
back: Strong/strong neutral; strong acid/weak base acidic; weak acid/strong base basic.

front: (HL) Half-equivalence point?
back: [HA] = [A⁻] so pH = pKa.

front: (HL) Choosing an indicator?
back: Its colour-change range must fall within the steep part of the pH curve.

front: (HL) Buffer and its pH?
back: Weak acid + conjugate base; pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

front: Amphiprotic species (with examples)?
back: Can both donate and accept a proton: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻. (Amphoteric is the wider term: reacts as acid and base.)

front: Conjugate pairs in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻?
back: NH₄⁺/NH₃ and H₂O/OH⁻. Water acts as the acid here.

front: Change in [H⁺] for a change of 1 pH unit?
back: Factor of 10 (log scale): pH 3 has 10× the [H⁺] of pH 4.

front: Common strong acids and bases?
back: Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ (first proton). Strong bases: group 1 hydroxides, Ba(OH)₂.

front: Common weak acids and bases?
back: Weak acids: carboxylic acids (CH₃COOH), H₂CO₃. Weak bases: NH₃ and amines (CH₃NH₂).

front: Strong vs concentrated?
back: Strong/weak: degree of ionisation. Concentrated/dilute: amount of acid per dm³. A dilute strong acid is possible.

front: Distinguishing a strong from a weak acid of equal concentration?
back: Strong: lower pH, higher conductivity, faster reaction with Mg/CaCO₃. Both need the same volume of base to neutralise.

front: pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl and of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ NaOH (298 K)?
(HL) pOH and its relation to pH?
back: pOH = −log₁₀[OH⁻]; pH + pOH = pKw = 14.00 at 298 K.

front: (HL) Why does pure water’s pH fall as temperature rises, yet it stays neutral?
back: Ionisation of water is endothermic, so Kw rises and [H⁺] increases; but [H⁺] = [OH⁻] still, so it remains neutral.

front: (HL) pKa and acid strength?
back: pKa = −log₁₀Ka. Smaller pKa (larger Ka) → stronger acid.

front: (HL) Kb for a weak base B?
back: B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻; Kb = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B]; [OH⁻] ≈ √(Kb·c).

front: (HL) Assumptions in calculating pH of a weak acid?
back: [H⁺] = [A⁻] (water ionisation negligible) and [HA]eq ≈ [HA]initial (ionisation small).

front: (HL) Features of a strong acid–strong base pH curve?
back: Starts ~pH 1; steep vertical section ~pH 3–11; equivalence point at pH 7.

front: (HL) Features of a weak acid–strong base pH curve?
back: Starts higher (~pH 3), buffer region, half-equivalence pH = pKa, short steep section ~pH 7–11, equivalence point > 7.

front: (HL) Features of a strong acid–weak base titration (acid added to base)?
back: Starts ~pH 11, buffer region, equivalence point < 7 (steep ~pH 3–7). Use methyl orange.

front: (HL) Methyl orange vs phenolphthalein?
back: Methyl orange (range ~3.1–4.4): strong acid–weak base. Phenolphthalein (~8.3–10.0): weak acid–strong base. Either for strong–strong.

front: (HL) How does an acid–base indicator work?
back: It is a weak acid HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ where HIn and In⁻ have different colours; the end point is near pH = pKa(HIn).

front: (HL) How does a CH₃COOH/CH₃COO⁻ buffer resist pH change?
back: Added H⁺ reacts with CH₃COO⁻ → CH₃COOH; added OH⁻ reacts with CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O; ratio [A⁻]/[HA] barely changes.

front: (HL) Making a buffer by partial neutralisation?
back: Add strong base to excess weak acid (e.g. 2 mol CH₃COOH + 1 mol NaOH) so both HA and A⁻ remain — gives pH = pKa at 1 : 1.

front: (HL) Effect of dilution on buffer pH?
back: pH barely changes (ratio [A⁻]/[HA] unchanged), but buffer capacity decreases.

front: (HL) Why is sodium ethanoate solution basic?
back: CH₃COO⁻ (conjugate base of a weak acid) accepts protons from water: CH₃COO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COOH + OH⁻.
